splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability about potential withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data even if the measurement date has passed.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during periods of absconding, so the supervisory period is extended by the time the individual was a fugitive.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled during absconding because no statutory provision authorizes tolling, and the term expires as specified in the judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars claims previously presented — when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are barred from raising any previously presented claim, on top of § 2255(h)'s separate requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the § 2244(b)(1) bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing a categorical prohibition in addition to § 2255(h) requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to state election procedures. Some circuits recognize candidate standing based on competitive injury, while others have imposed stricter requirements. The outcome affects whether election rule challenges can be brought before elections or are funneled into post-election litigation.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when challenging election rules that allegedly dilute lawful votes or change election procedures.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge state election procedures because the alleged injury is too speculative or generalized before the election occurs.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have developed differing approaches to discrimination claims in hospitality and business settings, including standards for liability and available remedies. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve a split involving the Second Circuit's approach to these questions, which could impact hospitality, retail, and other service industries nationwide.

positions.label: Second Circuit's approach
positions.summary: Applied a standard for discrimination claims in hospitality settings that the Supreme Court found sufficiently unsettled to warrant review, suggesting the approach may differ from other circuits.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits have applied different or more established standards for evaluating discrimination and fair treatment claims against business operators.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations in criminal sentencing contexts.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should apply the rule of lenity before deferring to agency interpretations of ambiguous criminal statutes or sentencing guidelines. At least three circuits hold lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit held deference trumps lenity. The split implicates fundamental questions about how criminal laws are construed after Loper Bright overruled Chevron.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity must be applied before deferring to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations of ambiguous criminal provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes priority over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, allowing authoritative agency interpretations to control.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) means 'and' or 'or.' The Ninth and Eleventh Circuits hold defendants are disqualified only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, while the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits hold that any single criterion is disqualifying. This split produces dramatically different sentences for identically situated defendants depending on geography.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' conjunctively.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or' or distributively.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is entitled to deference when the guideline text itself does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the career-offender guideline's commentary (Application Note 1) validly expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and other inchoate offenses, given that the guideline text is silent on inchoate offenses. Some circuits defer to the commentary under Stinson, while others hold the text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the career-offender guideline under Stinson and Kisor, and conspiracy qualifies as a controlled substance offense for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and the commentary impermissibly expands the definition, so conspiracy does not qualify as a controlled substance offense for career-offender purposes.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule includes substances not listed in the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally controlled. Some circuits hold the definition encompasses any state drug offense regardless of federal scheduling, while others require the substance to be on the federal schedule. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements.

positions.label: State schedule controls — no federal-law limitation
positions.summary: Holds that there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation onto the career-offender guideline, so state drug offenses qualify even if the substance is not federally scheduled.

positions.label: Federal schedule controls
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive sentencing reforms can contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. The Eighth Circuit categorically held they cannot, while other circuits have allowed such changes (alone or in combination with other factors) to support compassionate release. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) attempted to resolve this but its authority to do so is itself disputed.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive sentencing changes may be considered, at least in combination with other factors, as extraordinary and compelling reasons warranting a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to sanctioning the breach of trust.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts revoking supervised release may impose sentences to punish the underlying violative conduct or only to sanction the breach of the court's trust. The Sixth Circuit's precedent in United States v. Lewis allows express punishment at revocation, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split and raising questions about the statutory purpose of revocation proceedings.

positions.label: Courts may punish at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences to punish defendants for their supervised release violations, not merely to sanction the breach of trust.

positions.label: Revocation limited to sanctioning breach of trust
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be calibrated to the seriousness of the breach of trust, not to punish the defendant for the underlying conduct constituting the violation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to an appeal from an order on a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees, though filed in a criminal case, is a civil matter for purposes of the appeal deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because the motion is ancillary to the criminal case, but acknowledged a lopsided circuit split on the issue.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the longer civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) governs.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that the shorter criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies because the Hyde Amendment motion arises in and is part of the criminal case.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 is available to challenge conditions or terms of confinement (such as BOP transfer decisions), or whether it is limited to challenges to the fact or duration of confinement.
splits.description: Since Preiser v. Rodriguez, circuits have been split on whether habeas extends only to challenges to the fact or duration of confinement or also reaches challenges to conditions and terms of confinement such as BOP decisions on prerelease custody transfers. This longstanding split affects federal prisoners' ability to challenge BOP administrative decisions, including First Step Act earned-time-credit applications.

positions.label: Habeas available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus may be used to challenge conditions or terms of confinement, not just the fact or duration of imprisonment, when the prisoner seeks relief from specific unlawful restraints.

positions.label: Habeas limited to fact/duration of confinement
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is available only to challenge the fact or duration of confinement, and challenges to conditions must be brought through civil rights actions or other statutory vehicles.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the estate or the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that appreciation inures to the estate, creating a split with circuits that read § 348(f)(1)(A) as protecting debtors' post-petition equity gains upon good-faith conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A) and § 541(a)'s broad definition of estate property means post-petition appreciation in value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) was designed to protect good-faith converting debtors, and post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor, not the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine as an order effectively unreviewable on appeal from final judgment.
splits.description: Circuits have taken different approaches to whether denial of motions to seal medical records qualifies for immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine. The D.C. Circuit held that medical privacy is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate review, while other circuits have been less receptive to collateral order appeals in sealing contexts.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order that warrants immediate appellate review when a motion to seal is denied, because the privacy interest cannot be vindicated after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are generally not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because they can be reviewed on appeal from final judgment or protected through other means.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA permits suits for money damages against prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits allow such suits while others hold that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages, raising questions about the scope of Congressional spending power to impose personal liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA allows individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA authorizes suits for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities, as the statute's text is broad enough to encompass such claims.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Landor v. Louisiana Dep't of Corrections

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and Spending Clause legislation cannot impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
